headline: The Pentagon will livestream a firing squad.
summary: Nidal Hasan, the Army psychiatrist who shot 13 people dead at Fort Hood in 2009, will be executed by firing squad there on December 3. The Pentagon said Thursday it will livestream it. It is the first military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since 1945. Hegseth: "people need to understand that there's serious consequences."

cover_question.q: Do people have to watch it?

cover_answer: No. Nobody is made to watch, and we won't.
table_question: Should a punishment ever have an audience?

5-7.script: A man who was a soldier killed 13 people at an Army base in Texas in 2009, before you were born. A court said he must die for it, and in December soldiers will carry that out. The Army says it will show it on a screen, and nobody has to watch. We won't, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Shielded. If it reaches them: before you were born, and nobody has to watch.
5-7.why_long: Shielded: a six-year-old can do nothing with an execution, and takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives no method and no picture, only that it happened before they were born and that nobody has to watch. Cantor's work says what frightens this age is what it can see, so the screen stays off. Expect "will you watch?" No.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 2009 Army Major Nidal Hasan shot 13 people dead at Fort Hood, Texas. A court sentenced him to death in 2013. Military law needs the appeals done and the president's approval, a referee checking each step before the whistle. Trump gave it. The firing squad is set for December 3, now with a livestream.
8-12.why: The checklist before the whistle, then the new step: the camera.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults follow them, so the script hands them the chain military law lays out: a conviction, the appeals, the president's signature, a date. The referee's checklist is a mechanism they know. The camera is the one new rule. Expect "why would anyone watch?" Hegseth says so people see the consequences.

13-17.script: Should a punishment have an audience? The Pentagon will livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 soldiers at Fort Hood. Hegseth: "people need to understand that there's serious consequences." Second: in January Trump said he stopped Iran hanging people.
13-17.why: An audience for a punishment. Then the Iran line.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a court found Hasan guilty of 13 killings and the law allows the sentence, and the government that will broadcast it spent January warning Iran against public executions. The script gives Hegseth's reason in his words and asks whether both stand. Expect "would you watch?" Answer, then ask them.

5-7.q: Do people have to watch it?
5-7.a: No. Nobody is made to watch, and we won't. It is on a screen that can stay off.

8-12.q: Why do they want people to see it?
8-12.a: Hegseth says people need to understand there are consequences.
The Army hasn't said how it will run it. The last was in 1945.

13-17.q: Should a punishment have an audience?
13-17.a: Hegseth says yes, so people see the consequences. Last public one: 1936.

13-17.q: Didn't Trump tell Iran not to do this?
13-17.a: In January he said he stopped Iran hanging protesters.
